title: Under the Tuscan Sun
full_review:
Diane Lane elevates "Under the Tuscan Sun" (Touchstone) from a predictable fairy tale to an enjoyable but standard yarn about a woman rediscovering who she is by tasting a bit of the dolce vita.

Based loosely on the travel memoir by Frances Mayes, writer-director Audrey Wells' story is about triumphing over heartbreak and once again finding hope in life. Lane plays Frances, a San Francisco author who has just gone through a devastating -- and utterly surprising -- divorce. After some convincing by her friend Patti (Sandra Oh), Frances decides to take a trip to Florence, where she impulsively buys a dilapidated (naturally) Tuscan villa. The obvious parallel is that as Frances restores the house her soul is also renewed.

While the idea about a divorced woman comes from Wells, the renovating mishaps are from Mayes' book, in which the autobiographical heroine is happily married. However, the film's story remains grounded, enlivened occasionally by beautiful Italian vistas as well as a few mouth-watering feasts where long tables are crammed with colorful dishes.

The conventional story line shows Frances moping and looking pitiful as she wanders through the charming, ramshackle home. Then her spirits are slowly lifted as she begins to find her own rhythm again. She finally soars with the onset of a romance with Italian hunk Marcello (Raoul Bova) from a few towns over. This doomed romance, however, puts a huge strain on the film with its awkward dialogue and the unlikely difficulties the separated lovers encounter in meeting again.

Some of the plot threads require suspension of disbelief, such as Frances' ability to restore the three-bedroom house -- or even afford living expenses -- when her cheating ex-husband has taken pretty much all she had. However, Lane rescues the film with her appealing performance. She is attractive and natural as she plays the fantasy role of a woman escaping her troubles while picking olives and sipping Chianti.

Catholic viewers may be bothered by the character of Patti, a pregnant lesbian whose lover leaves her. Although Patti's homosexuality is not a major part of the story, nor is it flaunted in the film, the implied acceptance of her lifestyle may nonetheless be unsettling. However, it is noteworthy that the film emphasizes how good a friend Patti is to Frances when the forlorn woman is in need -- and vice versa.

Conversely, Catholics may be interested in a mildly developed plot thread that has Frances, a self-declared fallen-away Methodist, increasingly appreciating the Virgin Mary and in small ways considering life through the prism of faith. All this comes as she begins to see the meaning of family also through a different perspective.

Wells manages to tie up the loose plot strands into a neat package with the film's implausible but happy ending. So while "Under the Tuscan Sun" is no great cinematic accomplishment, it is nonetheless a tolerable two hours.

Because of an implied sexual encounter, references to a lesbian relationship, an instance of rough language and profanity with brief crass words, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
